questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Classify returns to scale from an input-output comparison
questions.stem: Ticket #1042: A team doubles labor and capital; output triples. Classify returns to scale.

options.text: Increasing returns: output rises more than inputs
Decreasing returns: output rises less than inputs
options.misconception: assumes scale always raises unit cost

options.text: Constant returns: output rises exactly with inputs
Negative returns: output falls when inputs rise

questions.explanation: Output triples while inputs double, so output rises more than inputs, indicating increasing returns. The tempting proportional rule would only fit constant returns.
questions.hint: Compare the output ratio to the input ratio.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a level from a growth rate
questions.stem: Ticket #1043: GDP level is 100 and grows 2% yearly. What is the growth rate, not the level?

options.text: 100, because that is the current GDP level
2%, because output rises two percent per year
102, because level plus growth equals rate

questions.explanation: The growth rate is the percentage change per period, here 2%, while 100 is the level. Adding them or treating level as rate is a common mix-up.
questions.hint: Ask whether the value is a stock or a flow.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Ticket #1044: Why does technological progress sustain growth while capital alone cannot?

answer.exemplar: Capital faces diminishing returns, so extra capital yields smaller output gains over time; technological progress shifts the production function upward and keeps per-worker output rising without bound.

questions.explanation: Diminishing returns to capital limit growth from capital deepening alone. Technology raises productivity at every capital level, sustaining long-run per-capita growth.
questions.hint: Contrast diminishing returns with shifting production.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Ticket #1045: With s=0.2, A=1, delta=0.1, n=0.05, find steady-state k=(sA/(n+delta))^(1/(1-alpha)) with alpha=0.3.
questions.explanation: Steady state requires investment equals break-even investment. Substituting gives k around 4.0. Rounding or using the wrong exponent changes the result.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Ticket #1046: Capital stock is 200 and depreciation rate is 10%. How much capital depreciates?
questions.explanation: Depreciation equals rate times stock, 0.10*200=20. Using the net rate or adding investment would be wrong.
questions.hint: Multiply stock by the depreciation rate.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Ticket #1047: Which capital level maximizes steady-state consumption per worker?

options.text: The level where investment is zero
The level where capital is largest possible
The level where MPK equals the depreciation rate
The level where savings rate is 100%

questions.explanation: Golden rule sets marginal product of capital equal to depreciation plus population growth. Maximizing capital or saving would starve consumption.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Ticket #1048: A model shows constant returns to a reproducible factor. What growth implication follows?

options.text: Sustained growth is possible without diminishing returns

questions.explanation: Constant returns to a reproducible factor allow sustained growth. Diminishing returns would eventually halt it, but that is not this case.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why property rights foster investment
questions.stem: Ticket #1049: How do secure property rights encourage capital accumulation?

answer.exemplar: When investors expect to keep returns, they are willing to save and invest in capital; insecure rights reduce expected returns and discourage accumulation.

questions.explanation: Secure rights raise expected returns to investment. Without them, savers fear expropriation and underinvest, slowing capital accumulation.
questions.hint: Link security of returns to willingness to invest.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Assess contract enforcement's role in investment
questions.stem: Ticket #1050: If weak enforcement lowers investment by 15% on a base of 100 units, what is investment?
questions.explanation: Investment falls 15% of 100, leaving 85. Adding 15 or taking 15 of the new level would be wrong.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Ticket #1051: Investment I=0.15Y with Y=200. Compute I.
questions.explanation: 0.15 times 200 equals 30. Using 15% of 100 or misplacing the decimal gives the wrong value.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Ticket #1052: How does corruption most directly reduce growth?

options.text: It raises the effective cost of investment

questions.explanation: Corruption acts like a tax on investment, raising effective costs and discouraging capital formation. It does not lower prices or remove depreciation.
questions.hint: Think of corruption as an extra cost.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Ticket #1053: Public roads raise private output by 5%. What is the mechanism?
questions.explanation: Public capital complements private capital, raising its productivity. It does not substitute for or reduce private capital.
questions.hint: Public capital works alongside private capital.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Compute investment from saving and capital flows
questions.stem: Ticket #1054: Saving S=120, capital inflow KI=30. Investment I=S+KI. Compute I.
questions.explanation: In an open economy, investment equals saving plus net capital inflow, 120+30=150. Subtracting would confuse direction.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Ticket #1055: A team doubles all inputs; output rises 50%. Classify returns.

options.text: Constant returns because scale is uniform
Decreasing returns because output rises less

questions.explanation: Output rises 50% while inputs double, so output rises less than inputs, indicating decreasing returns. A mere output rise is not increasing returns.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Compute a growth rate from two levels
questions.stem: Ticket #1056: Level rises from 100 to 110. Compute growth rate (110-100)/100.
questions.explanation: Growth rate is change over initial level, (110-100)/100=0.10. Using 110 as denominator gives the wrong rate.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Identify the driver of sustained growth
questions.stem: Ticket #1057: Which factor best sustains per-capita growth in the long run?
questions.explanation: Technological progress sustains per-capita growth; capital deepening faces diminishing returns. Higher depreciation or population growth do not sustain it.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Ticket #1058: What condition defines the steady state in a growth model?

answer.exemplar: In steady state, capital per worker is constant, so investment per worker equals break-even investment covering depreciation and population growth.

questions.explanation: Steady state means no change in capital per worker, so investment matches depreciation plus population growth. Without that equality, capital per worker drifts.
questions.hint: Set change in capital per worker to zero.

provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Ticket #1059: Gross investment is 50, depreciation is 20. Compute net investment.
questions.explanation: Net investment equals gross minus depreciation, 50-20=30. Adding them or using gross alone is wrong.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Ticket #1060: Given f(k)=k^0.3, delta+n=0.1, golden rule sets MPK=delta+n. Find k where 0.3*k^-0.7=0.1.
questions.explanation: Solving 0.3*k^-0.7=0.1 gives k about 4.73. Arithmetic or exponent errors change the answer.
questions.hint: Solve for k using the marginal product.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Ticket #1061: In an AK model, what does constant returns to capital imply?

options.text: Growth rate is independent of saving
Growth rate depends on the savings rate

questions.explanation: In an AK model, the growth rate is proportional to the savings rate because returns do not diminish. Neoclassical models make growth independent of saving in steady state.
questions.hint: No diminishing returns ties growth to saving.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Ticket #1062: Secure rights raise investment from 80 to 100. Compute percentage increase.
questions.explanation: Percentage increase is (100-80)/80=0.25 or 25%. Dividing by 100 gives the wrong 20%.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Ticket #1063: Why does better contract enforcement expand credit access?

answer.exemplar: Reliable enforcement lowers lender risk, so lenders offer more credit at lower rates, letting firms borrow and invest more.

questions.explanation: Enforcement reduces default risk, lowering interest rates and expanding borrowing. Without it, lenders ration credit.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Ticket #1064: Country A has stronger institutions than B. What follows for investment?
questions.explanation: Stronger institutions raise expected returns and lower risk, boosting investment. The reverse or no-effect claims ignore that channel.

questions.stem: Ticket #1065: A bribe adds 10% to a 500 cost. Compute total cost.
questions.explanation: Total cost is 500 plus 10%, 500*1.10=550. Adding 10 units or 50 would be wrong.

questions.stem: Ticket #1066: Public capital share is 20% of total capital 500. Compute public capital.
questions.explanation: 20% of 500 is 100. Using 20 units or 20% of output would be wrong.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Ticket #1067: In an open economy, why can investment exceed domestic saving?

answer.exemplar: Capital inflows from abroad finance the gap, so investment equals domestic saving plus net foreign capital inflow.

questions.explanation: Foreign capital inflows finance investment beyond domestic saving. Closed-economy equality does not hold.

questions.stem: Ticket #1068: A team doubles all inputs; output doubles. Classify returns.

options.text: Constant returns because output matches inputs

questions.explanation: Output doubles with inputs, so constant returns. A mere rise or cost change does not change the classification.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish level and rate in data
questions.stem: Ticket #1069: A chart shows GDP level 500 and growth 3%. Which is the rate?
questions.explanation: 3% is the growth rate; 500 is the level. Adding them mixes units.

questions.stem: Ticket #1070: Productivity grows 2% and population 1%. Approx per-capita growth?
questions.explanation: Per-capita growth roughly equals productivity growth minus population growth, 2-1=1%. Ignoring population overstates it.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Ticket #1072: Why must gross investment exceed depreciation to grow capital?

answer.exemplar: Net investment equals gross minus depreciation; only positive net investment adds to the capital stock.

questions.explanation: Capital stock grows only when gross investment exceeds replacement. Otherwise net investment is zero or negative.
questions.hint: Net investment drives capital stock change.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Ticket #1073: Golden rule condition equates MPK to what?
questions.explanation: Golden rule sets MPK equal to depreciation plus population growth. Savings rate is a policy variable, not the condition.
questions.hint: Match marginal product to break-even rate.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Ticket #1075: A country strengthens property rights. Expected investment response?
questions.explanation: Stronger rights raise expected returns, encouraging investment. The reverse or no-effect claims ignore that channel.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Ticket #1077: How do institutions affect long-run growth?

answer.exemplar: Institutions shape incentives for saving, investment, and innovation; better institutions raise expected returns and sustain growth.

questions.explanation: Institutions set the rules that determine investment and innovation incentives. Better rules raise expected returns and growth.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Ticket #1078: Corruption is best modeled as what for investors?
questions.explanation: Corruption raises effective costs, acting like a tax on investment. It is not a subsidy or productivity boost.

questions.stem: Ticket #1083: Which does NOT sustain per-capita growth indefinitely?

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Ticket #1084: In steady state, what happens to capital per worker?

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Ticket #1086: Why does over-accumulating capital reduce consumption?

answer.exemplar: Beyond the golden rule, extra capital's marginal product falls below break-even cost, so maintaining it crowds out consumption.

questions.explanation: Past the golden rule, marginal product is below break-even cost, so maintaining capital reduces consumption. Under-accumulation has the opposite problem.

questions.stem: Ticket #1087: What feature defines an AK growth model?
questions.explanation: AK models have constant returns to capital. Diminishing returns define neoclassical models.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Ticket #1091: Why does corruption discourage investment?

answer.exemplar: Corruption raises expected costs and uncertainty, lowering expected returns, so fewer projects clear the hurdle rate.

questions.explanation: Corruption acts as a tax and raises uncertainty, reducing expected returns below hurdle rates. Projects are then abandoned.

questions.stem: Ticket #1092: Which is an example of public capital?

questions.explanation: Level is a stock at a point; growth rate is change over time. A large economy can grow slowly, and vice versa.
